By Josh Pilcher · New reports Tuesday and Friday evenings

The parks are the company now. Cinderella Castle at dusk, seen down a full Main Street. The media empire still matters, but it matters the way a supplier matters: it feeds the places people pay to stand in.

Latest Report · Tuesday, November 10, 2026

What Is Disney Anymore?

Five years ago the market priced Disney as the future of television. It fell 60 percent anyway. This is an autopsy: what the company actually is now, why the fall happened, and whether the price on the body is right.

Disney is no longer the company the market was pricing at $200 in 2021. It is a parks and cruise business that earned $10 billion last year, with a streaming service attached that finally turns a profit, and a television business that is melting underneath it at about half a billion dollars of profit a year. The stock’s fall from $202 to $79 was mostly the market repricing a growth story that was never going to arrive on schedule, not the streaming losses themselves.

The earnings have since recovered, but the market has not re-rated the company, because the new earnings rest on price rises rather than volume, and the two engines that must replace television are a thin-margin streamer and a parks business that needs $60 billion of new investment to keep growing. At $119, the stock sits inside a fair-value band of roughly $111 to $125. The market has it about right, leaning modestly cheap if you believe the next two years of earnings guidance.

Priced between two kinds of company

Forward price to earnings, November 9, 2026. Disney is cheaper than the index it belongs to and cheaper than the streamer it is compared with, and much more expensive than the cable company it is starting to resemble.

Netflix, forward P/EDisney, forward P/EComcast, forward P/E

The gap between trailing and forward is the whole argument. On trailing earnings Disney trades at 24.6 times, almost exactly the S&P 500. On forward earnings it trades at 15.7 times, a discount of about 12 percent, because the denominator is growing fast. Whether that growth arrives is what the next two years decide.

Inside the Report
01 The Verdict

The Bottom Line

Disney is a parks and cruise business that earned $10 billion last year, with a profitable streamer attached and a television business melting at about half a billion dollars a year. At $119, the stock sits inside the fair-value band.

 $111 to $125Fair-value band→ 02 Chapter One

The Peak and the Fall

The stock did not drift down. It was repriced, in a specific order, for specific reasons. The price fell 57 percent to November 2022 while revenue rose: multiple compression, not earnings collapse.

 $201.91Peak, Mar 8, 2021→ 03 Chapter Two

What Disney Is Now

Follow the operating income and the company looks nothing like its reputation. Experiences earned $10.0 billion on $36.2 billion of revenue. Entertainment earned $4.7 billion. The profit engine has inverted.

 57%Of profit, from Experiences→ 04 Chapter Three

The Streaming Bet

The $4 billion hole is closed. What filled it was not growth. It was price, charged to fewer people: a swing of $4.75 billion in three years, to a 5.4 percent margin.

 $1.33BStreaming profit, FY2025→ 05 Chapter Four

The Parks Engine

Record profit, record prices, flat attendance. The engine runs on charging more to roughly the same number of people, and the answer is $60 billion of new capacity.

 $60BExperiences capital plan→ 06 Chapter Five

The Melting Legacy

Linear television built modern Disney. It is shrinking at a steady, ignorable pace, about $500 million of profit a year, which is exactly what makes it dangerous.

 $2.96BLinear profit, FY2025→ 07 Chapter Six

The IP Question

The flywheel made Disney different for seventy years: film to toy to ride to film. Management itself now says the machine was overworked. Disney owns the characters. YouTube owns the hours.

 13.1%YouTube share of US TV time→ 08 Chapter Seven

The Valuation

Cheap on the earnings that are coming, full price on the earnings that exist. The gap between those two sentences is the whole argument.

 15.7xForward P/E→ 09 Chapter Eight

Two Rival Reads

Two honest ways to read everything above. Remade and cheap, or fairly valued and maybe expensive. Each one names the evidence that would prove it.

 $135 to $150Read One fair value→ 10 Chapter Nine

Watchlist

Five things that settle the argument, in the order they arrive. The first is the fiscal fourth-quarter print on November 17, 2026.

The Two Engines

The parks print the money. Streaming finally turns a profit, at a thin margin. Everything else in the company is measured against those two facts.

Chapter Four · The Parks Engine

The engine runs on price, not volume

Experiences earned a record $10.0 billion in fiscal 2025 on record revenue of $36.2 billion. Domestic attendance fell 1 percent while per-guest spending rose 5 percent, and management says the domestic parks are essentially at capacity.

$10.0B Experiences operating income, FY2025
$36.2B Experiences revenue, FY2025 Read the Parks section → Chapter Three · The Streaming Bet

Profitable now, on new terms

The service makes money. It also charges three times its launch price to fewer subscribers than it had in 2022, and the company no longer reports how many subscribers there are. The margin is 5.4 percent, against Netflix at 29.5 percent.

$1.33B Streaming profit, FY2025

THE BOARDPURPOSE

Why The Board exists.

By Josh Pilcher · New reports Tuesday and Friday evenings

I don’t have a ton of time. It’s hard to keep up.

There are so many conflicting narratives, fed by conflicting interests. It feels hard to know what is true, and I know I’m not alone in that.

I often have questions I want answered, or things I don’t understand, that the news simply doesn’t cover. Not all of the time, but sometimes. When that happens, there is nowhere obvious to go for a straight answer.

In my ideal world, I build something useful to me. Something I enjoy reading. Because if I do, so will other people, and it will help them too.

What that looks like in a year, who knows.

The Board is a personal project. Everything here reflects my own views and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or representative of my employer.

From the Latest Report

What to watch next

Five things that settle the argument, in the order they arrive:

  1. 1Nov 17, 2026 · Fiscal fourth-quarter resultsThe streaming margin for the full year against the 10 percent guide, and whether fiscal 2027 double-digit earnings growth is reaffirmed. This report publishes before that print.
  2. 2Streaming margin and disclosureDoes Disney resume subscriber disclosure, and does the streaming margin hold above 10 percent without another price rise? Margin that survives a quiet pricing year is real margin.
  3. 3Parks volume against priceDomestic attendance and per-capita spending, side by side with Universal’s Orlando numbers, and whether the $60 billion of capital spending earns its cost of capital as the new capacity opens.
  4. 4The linear melt rateQuarterly Linear Networks operating income. Does the decline stay near $500 million a year, or accelerate past $700 million? The whole valuation leans on the answer.
  5. 5Succession under D’AmaroHis first full year as sole chief executive in fiscal 2027, after Iger leaves on December 31, 2026: the studio slate, the streaming margin, and whether Walden stays in the creative chief role.
